lessons.title: Classifying data and using tables
lessons.summary: Classify categories, counts and measurements. Organise observations in tally and two-way tables.
lessons.objective: Classify categories, counts and measurements. Organise observations in tally and two-way tables.
lessons.before: Count repeated observations and add or subtract whole numbers.
lessons.ideas:
Qualitative data name categories. Numerical data are discrete when counted in separated steps and continuous when measured on a scale.

Choose a category for every observation, tally each observation once, and record the number of marks as the frequency.

Add across a row to combine columns. Add down a column to combine rows. Subtract known parts from a total to recover a missing cell.
lessons.method:
How do I tell categories, counts and measurements apart?

A variable is a feature recorded for each person or object. Some variables name a category. Others record a number.

How can I avoid missing or double-counting observations?

A tally records one mark for every observation. Keep marks in groups of five so that you can count them quickly.

Which totals help me complete a two-way table?

A two-way table classifies the same observations by two features. A data cell is counted once in each relevant total.
mistakes: A number used as a label, such as a postcode, describes a category. Adding the labels would have no interpretation.
The number of categories is not the number of observations.
Do not add a subtotal twice when you find the grand total.

examples.title: Classify a recorded variable
examples.question:
In a class survey, a learner records the type of classroom device. Which type of data is recorded?

  1. All three
  2. Qualitative
  3. Discrete numerical
  4. Continuous numerical
examples.solution:
A device type is a category.

Answer Qualitative.

examples.title: Convert observations into a tally and frequency
examples.question:
The colours of some cards were recorded in this order.

Green, Orange, Blue, Red, Green, Orange, Red, Green, Orange, Red, Orange.

Find the frequency of red.
examples.solution:
Count the observations in each colour once.

ColourTallyFrequency
Green|||\(3\)
Orange||||\(4\)
Blue|\(1\)
Red|||\(3\)

Answer \(3\).

examples.title: Use a two-way table to recover a count
examples.question:
The two-way table classifies journeys by time and mode of travel.

TimeWalkBusTotal
Morning\(12\)\(3\)\(15\)
Afternoon?\(7\)\(15\)
Total\(20\)\(10\)\(30\)

Find the missing frequency.
examples.solution:
A row total counts all modes at one time. A column total counts one mode across both times.

\(8=15-7\)

Answer \(8\).

lessons.title: Mean, median, mode and range
lessons.summary: Find each average and the range of an ungrouped list, then choose the measure that answers the question.
lessons.objective: Find each average and the range of an ungrouped list, then choose the measure that answers the question.
lessons.before: Add numbers, divide a total into equal parts and order values.
lessons.ideas:
Divide the sum of all recorded values by the number of observations. You can recover the total by multiplying the mean by the sample size.

For an odd number of values take the one in the middle. For an even number take the mean of the middle two. Range is maximum minus minimum.

Use the mode for a most-popular category. Use the median when extreme values would make the mean unrepresentative. Use the mean when the full total matters.
lessons.method:
How do I share a total equally?

The mean describes how much each observation would have if the total were shared equally.

Which positions give the median and range?

The median sits in the middle of the ordered values. The range measures the gap from smallest to largest.

Which average answers the question?

Mode describes what occurs most often, median describes the ordered middle, and mean includes every value.
mistakes: If one observation equals zero it is still included in the number you divide by.
Removing repeated values changes the positions and can change the median.
The range is a measure of spread. It does not describe a typical value.

examples.title: Calculate the mean of listed data
examples.question:
A learner records these daily scores.

\(11,\;14,\;7,\;9,\;8,\;10,\;21\).

Find the exact mean.

examples.title: Find the median after ordering
examples.question: Find the median of \(9,\;11,\;18,\;10,\;13,\;22\).
examples.solution:
In order the values are \(9,\;10,\;11,\;13,\;18,\;22\).

The middle values are \(11\) and \(13\). Take their mean.

Answer \(12\).

examples.title: Find the most frequent value
examples.question: Find the mode of \(6,\;9,\;6,\;4,\;17,\;9,\;6,\;11\).
examples.solution:
\(6\) appears three times. Other values appear fewer times.

Answer \(6\).

lessons.title: Frequency tables and comparing samples
lessons.summary: Use ungrouped frequencies for averages and compare samples without drawing unsupported conclusions.
lessons.objective: Use ungrouped frequencies for averages and compare samples without drawing unsupported conclusions.
lessons.before: Find the mean, median and range of a short ordered list.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply every value by its frequency. Add the products and divide by the sum of the frequencies.

Add counts to locate the class or value of the middle position. At an even sample size, check whether the two central positions are in different rows.

Compare like measures and comparable units. State which group has the larger centre or spread and limit a conclusion to what the data support.
lessons.method:
How does a frequency table represent repeated observations?

A table with one row for each value compresses the list without losing how often each value occurred.

How can I find the middle without rewriting the full list?

Each frequency occupies that many consecutive positions in the ordered dataset.

What can I conclude about two groups?

A higher median describes a higher typical value. A larger range describes a wider gap between the sample extremes.
mistakes: Dividing by the number of rows gives equal weight to different frequencies.
The cumulative count is an observation position, not the value of the observation.
A small or unrepresentative sample cannot establish the same pattern in an entire population.

examples.title: Find a mean from an ungrouped frequency table
examples.question:
Number of visitsFrequency
\(3\)\(6\)
\(4\)\(2\)
\(6\)\(8\)
\(8\)\(2\)

Find the mean number of visits. Give an exact answer.
examples.solution:
VisitsFrequencyValue × frequency
\(3\)\(6\)\(18\)
\(4\)\(2\)\(8\)
\(6\)\(8\)\(48\)
\(8\)\(2\)\(16\)

\(\text{Mean}=\frac{90}{18}=5\)

Answer \(5\).

examples.title: Locate the middle position in a frequency table
examples.question:
Number of visitsFrequency
\(5\)\(3\)
\(6\)\(3\)
\(8\)\(10\)
\(10\)\(2\)

Find the median number of visits.
examples.solution:
The total number of observations is \(18\).

VisitsRunning total
\(5\)\(3\)
\(6\)\(6\)
\(8\)\(16\)
\(10\)\(18\)

Use the running totals to locate both central observations.

Answer \(8\).

examples.title: Compare median values between groups
examples.question:
GroupRecorded times (min)
A\(12,\;14,\;16,\;18\)
B\(12,\;16,\;16,\;20\)

By how many minutes is the median of B higher than the median of A?
examples.solution:
Take the middle two observations of each ordered group.

\(\text{Difference}=16-15=1\)

Answer \(1\).

lessons.title: Bar charts and pictograms
lessons.summary: Read and construct single, dual and stacked bar charts and use whole and half symbols in pictograms.
lessons.objective: Read and construct single, dual and stacked bar charts and use whole and half symbols in pictograms.
lessons.before: Read a labelled frequency scale and add or compare counts.
lessons.ideas:
Use a consistent scale starting at zero. Draw equal-width bars to the heights shown by the frequencies.

For a dual bar chart read each group's height from zero. For a stacked bar chart subtract the bottom of a segment from its top to recover its own count.

Multiply the number of whole symbols by the key. Add the correct fraction of the key for each part-symbol.
lessons.method:
How does a single bar show a count?

A bar chart shows frequencies for categories or separate discrete values. The bars have equal width, with gaps between categories.

When should I read two separate heights or one segment?

Dual bars place two groups next to each other. Stacked bars combine groups in separate segments of one bar.

What does each symbol in a pictogram count?

A pictogram shows a frequency with repeated symbols. A key says how many observations one complete symbol represents.
mistakes: The thickness of a bar does not show a larger frequency.
The upper boundary of the second segment shows the combined total.
If one full symbol represents six observations then half a symbol represents three.

examples.title: Read a single bar chart
examples.question: Find the frequency of amber.
examples.solution:
Read the height of the amber bar using the frequency scale on the left.

Answer \(2\).

examples.title: Read a dual bar chart
examples.question: By how much do the two groups' red counts differ?
examples.solution:
The adjacent bars use the same vertical scale.

\(\text{Difference}=8-6=2\)

Answer \(2\).

examples.title: Use the pictogram key
examples.question: Find how many red items the pictogram represents.
examples.solution:
A half-symbol represents \(4\).

\(\text{Number of items}=\frac{8}{2}\times 8=32\)

Answer \(32\).

lessons.title: Pie charts and proportions
lessons.summary: Convert frequencies to sector angles, recover counts from sectors and compare proportions between groups.
lessons.objective: Convert frequencies to sector angles, recover counts from sectors and compare proportions between groups.
lessons.before: Find a part as a fraction of a total.
lessons.ideas:
Divide the category count by the total and multiply by \(360^\circ\). Draw every sector from the centre using a protractor.

Divide the sector angle by \(360^\circ\) and multiply by the total frequency. To complete a missing sector, subtract the other angles from a full turn.

Compare sector angles to compare shares. To compare actual counts, use the angle and the total for each pie.
lessons.method:
How do I turn a frequency into a sector angle?

A whole pie represents the entire sample. Each sector represents the same fraction of the circle as its category represents of the sample.

How do I recover a count from an angle?

An angle represents a fraction of the total sample. A right angle corresponds to one quarter.

Can I compare two pies if their totals differ?

A bigger angle means a bigger share. If two pies have different totals, the sector with the bigger angle need not contain more observations.
mistakes: The frequencies need not add to 360. The angles do.
An angle of \(60^\circ\) is one sixth of a whole circle, not 60 per cent.
A pie chart alone gives no sample size unless the total is shown.

examples.title: Calculate a sector angle
examples.question:
Travel modeNumber of journeys
Walk\(20\)
Bus\(24\)
Cycle\(28\)
Other\(48\)

What angle represents other journeys in a pie chart?
examples.solution:
\(\theta=\frac{48}{120}\times360^\circ=144^\circ\)

Answer \(144^\circ\).

examples.title: Recover a frequency from a sector angle
examples.question: This chart represents \(120\) journeys. Find the number of bus journeys.
examples.solution:
\(\text{Number}=\frac{72}{360}\times 120=24\)

Answer \(24\).

examples.title: Compare shares when group sizes differ
examples.question:
SurveyTotalWalking angle
A\(120\)\(84^\circ\)
B\(300\)\(66^\circ\)

Which survey has the greater proportion walking?

  1. The angles cannot tell us
  2. Survey A
  3. Survey B
  4. Both the same
examples.solution:
Compare the walking angles out of 360°. The larger angle shows the greater share. Comparing counts would require both totals.

Answer Survey A.

lessons.title: Stem-and-leaf diagrams
lessons.summary: Build an ordered diagram with a key, then use its leaves to find positions, counts and spread.
lessons.objective: Build an ordered diagram with a key, then use its leaves to find positions, counts and spread.
lessons.before: Read tens and units and order a list of whole numbers.
lessons.ideas:
With key \(3\mid4\) means \(34\), the entry \(4\mid2\) means \(42\). Each leaf is a separate observation.

Keep repeated leaves. Check the total number of leaves against the number of observations.

For a median, count to the middle position or positions across all rows. For the range, read the first and last values and subtract.
lessons.method:
How do the stem and leaf make a complete value?

The stem records the earlier digit or digits. The leaf is usually the last digit, but the key tells you the scale.

How do I build an ordered diagram?

Write the stems in increasing order. Put each leaf beside its stem and order the leaves from left to right.

How can I read a median, a range or a count quickly?

Read each complete value using the key. The leaves already preserve the ordering when the diagram is complete.
mistakes: A stem alone is not a complete data value.
A repeated value needs repeated leaves. It is not one extra stem.
For a strict threshold, leave out a leaf equal to the threshold.

examples.title: Use the key to read a stem and leaf
examples.question:
StemLeaves
\(5\)\(3\quad 3\quad 7\)
\(6\)\(2\quad 2\quad 4\)
\(7\)\(3\quad 8\)

Key \(5\mid 3\) means \(53\).

Read the largest value in the stem \(6\).
examples.solution:
Use the last ordered leaf of this stem and join it to the tens digit.

Answer \(64\).

examples.title: Complete one stem with ordered leaves
examples.question:
The data are \(27,\;32,\;35,\;48,\;21,\;23,\;32,\;40\). Choose the ordered leaves for the stem \(3\).

  1. 2 5 2
  2. 2 5
  3. 2 2 5 5
  4. 2 2 5
examples.solution:
Find every value with the required tens digit. Keep both copies of a repeated leaf.

StemLeaves
\(2\)\(1\quad 3\quad 7\)
\(3\)\(2\quad 2\quad 5\)
\(4\)\(0\quad 8\)

Key \(2\mid 1\) means \(21\).

Answer 2 2 5.

examples.title: Find the median in an ordered stem-and-leaf diagram
examples.question:
StemLeaves
\(4\)\(0\quad 3\quad 7\)
\(5\)\(2\quad 2\quad 5\)
\(6\)\(0\quad 8\)

Key \(4\mid 0\) means \(40\).

Find the median.
examples.solution:
There are eight leaves. Count to the fourth and fifth ones across all rows.

\(\text{Median}=\frac{104}{2}=52\)

Answer \(52\).

lessons.title: Scatter diagrams and lines of best fit
lessons.summary: Plot paired measurements, distinguish types of correlation and use a ruled line of best fit for an estimate.
lessons.objective: Plot paired measurements, distinguish types of correlation and use a ruled line of best fit for an estimate.
lessons.before: Plot a coordinate pair and read both axes of a graph.
lessons.ideas:
Read the x-variable, read its paired y-value from the same row, then plot the point with a small cross.

Use the whole set of points. Treat an unusual point as an observation and describe it separately when useful.

For an estimate, start at the given value, move to the line and read the other scale. The line need not pass through any recorded point.
lessons.method:
How do I plot paired data?

A scatter diagram shows two measurements for each individual. The scales can differ between axes.

What does the overall shape tell me?

A generally rising group suggests positive correlation. A falling group suggests negative correlation. A cloud without a clear linear direction shows little or no linear correlation.

Where do I draw a line of best fit?

Draw a line through the overall centre of the points, with a reasonable balance of points either side along the full observed range.
mistakes: Joining the crosses in sequence does not show a scatter trend.
Correlation describes association. It cannot by itself show that one measurement caused the other.
Outside the observed x-range the estimate is an extrapolation and is less reliable.

examples.title: Read a plotted pair
examples.question: How many items were recorded at \(8\) minutes?
examples.solution:
Read across from the point above the stated horizontal coordinate.

Answer \(16\).

examples.title: Identify the direction of correlation
examples.question:
Which description best fits the plot?

  1. Negative correlation
  2. No linear correlation
  3. One joined time-series line
  4. Positive correlation
examples.solution:
From left to right, the points generally show no consistent straight-line trend.

Answer No linear correlation.

examples.title: Use the drawn line of best fit
examples.question: Use the drawn line of best fit to estimate the number of items at \(3\) minutes.
examples.solution:
Move vertically from the given time to the line, then horizontally to the items scale.

Answer \(17\).

lessons.title: Quartiles and the interquartile range
lessons.summary: Find quartiles of ordered data and compare the middle spread with the full range.
lessons.objective: Find quartiles of ordered data and compare the middle spread with the full range.
lessons.before: Find the median of an ordered list with an odd or even number of observations.
lessons.ideas:
Split the ordered data into lower and upper halves. For the method used here, leave out the overall median if the number of values is odd.

Calculate \(\mathrm{IQR}=Q_3-Q_1\). A smaller IQR describes a narrower spread for the middle half.

Use the median and IQR for a comparison of typical values and central spread. Limit your conclusion to the recorded groups.
lessons.method:
Where are the quartiles in an ordered list?

Put the data in order. The lower quartile is the median of the lower half. The upper quartile is the median of the upper half.

How is the interquartile range different from the range?

The interquartile range gives the width between the lower and upper quartiles. The range gives the width of the whole ordered set.

What happens when an extreme value changes?

Changing only the maximum can increase the range greatly. The central quartiles may stay the same.
mistakes: Counting observations on the original unsorted list can put the quartile in the wrong place.
The interquartile range is not the number of observations between the quartiles.
Two sets can have the same median but different spreads. One measure does not describe an entire distribution.

examples.title: Find the lower quartile from ordered data
examples.question:
The values are \(8,\;9,\;14,\;20,\;7,\;8,\;13,\;16\).

Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

Find the lower quartile.
examples.solution:
Order the data as \(7,\;8,\;8,\;9,\;13,\;14,\;16,\;20\).

Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

The ordered lower half is \(7,\;8,\;8,\;9\).

Answer \(8\).

examples.title: Find the interquartile range from ordered data
examples.question:
The values are \(10,\;11,\;13,\;19,\;9,\;10,\;12,\;15\).

Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

Find the interquartile range.
examples.solution:
Order the data as \(9,\;10,\;10,\;11,\;12,\;13,\;15,\;19\).

Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

\(\text{IQR}=14-10=4\)

Answer \(4\).

examples.title: Find the median from ordered data
examples.question:
The values are \(12,\;13,\;17,\;23,\;11,\;12,\;16,\;19\).

Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

Find the median.
examples.solution:
Order the data as \(11,\;12,\;12,\;13,\;16,\;17,\;19,\;23\).

Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

Count to the central position or average the two middle values, according to the sample size.

Answer \(\frac{29}{2}\).

lessons.title: Estimated mean and modal class
lessons.summary: Use grouped frequencies to estimate a mean, locate a modal class and explain what the grouping hides.
lessons.objective: Use grouped frequencies to estimate a mean, locate a modal class and explain what the grouping hides.
lessons.before: Find a mean from an ungrouped frequency table.
lessons.ideas:
For a continuous interval add the two boundaries and halve. For a group of discrete integer values average the smallest and largest integers in the group.

Multiply each midpoint by its frequency. Add these products and divide by the sum of the frequencies.

Compare the frequency column and state the whole interval. For the modal-class questions here the intervals have equal width.
lessons.method:
What value represents a whole class?

A grouped table tells us how many observations fall within each class. The individual values are missing.

How do I estimate the mean from a table?

Use the midpoint of each class as a representative value for the observations within that class.

Which class is the most frequent?

The modal class names a class with greatest frequency. It does not identify an exact mode in the original observations.
mistakes: Class width and class midpoint answer different questions.
Dividing by the number of intervals ignores how many observations fall in each interval.
Reporting the largest frequency alone does not identify the class.

examples.title: Find the representative midpoint of a group
examples.question:
Time (min)Frequency
\(5<t\le 12\)\(4\)
\(12<t\le 18\)\(11\)
\(18<t\le 27\)\(12\)
\(27<t\le 37\)\(8\)

Find the midpoint of the class \(27<t\le 37\).
examples.solution:
\(\text{Midpoint}=\frac{27+37}{2}=32\)

Answer \(32\).

examples.title: Estimate a mean using class midpoints
examples.question:
Time (min)Frequency
\(2<t\le 9\)\(4\)
\(9<t\le 13\)\(9\)
\(13<t\le 22\)\(12\)
\(22<t\le 29\)\(6\)

Estimate the mean to 1 decimal place.
examples.solution:
Use each group's midpoint for the observations in that group.

ClassFrequencyMidpointMidpoint × frequency
\(2<t\le 9\)\(4\)\(\frac{11}{2}\)\(22\)
\(9<t\le 13\)\(9\)\(11\)\(99\)
\(13<t\le 22\)\(12\)\(\frac{35}{2}\)\(210\)
\(22<t\le 29\)\(6\)\(\frac{51}{2}\)\(153\)

\(\text{Estimate}=\frac{484}{31}\)

Answer \(15.6\) to 1 decimal place.

examples.title: Identify the most frequent class
examples.question:
Time (min)Frequency
\(11<t\le 16\)\(14\)
\(16<t\le 21\)\(4\)
\(21<t\le 26\)\(11\)
\(26<t\le 31\)\(7\)

Which is the modal class?

  1. \(26<t\le 31\)
  2. \(11<t\le 16\)
  3. \(16<t\le 21\)
  4. \(21<t\le 26\)
examples.solution:
The modal class is the interval with the greatest frequency. It does not identify an exact modal time.

Answer \(11<t\le 16\).

lessons.title: Constructing cumulative frequency diagrams
lessons.summary: Use running totals, plot them at the upper boundaries and work back to class counts.
lessons.objective: Use running totals, plot them at the upper boundaries and work back to class counts.
lessons.before: Read an inequality interval and find totals from a frequency table.
lessons.ideas:
Start at zero at the first lower boundary. Add one class frequency at a time until the final total equals the sample size.

Plot the initial lower boundary at zero. Finish at the full sample size and join the points using a smooth curve.

Subtract adjacent cumulative readings to find a class count. Subtract a reading from the final total to find a count above that boundary.
lessons.method:
What is the cumulative frequency at a boundary?

Cumulative frequency tells how many observations are at or below a given upper class boundary.

Which points do I plot?

Each point needs an upper boundary and its cumulative frequency. Mark the plotted points with clear crosses.

How can I recover counts above a boundary or inside a class?

A cumulative reading includes every observation up to the given boundary. It does not give a single class frequency directly.
mistakes: A class containing zero observations leaves the running total unchanged.
Class midpoints are used for estimating a mean. They are not the horizontal coordinates of these cumulative points.
Read ‘more than’ and ‘at most’ carefully before subtracting.

examples.title: Find a running total for a class boundary
examples.question:
Time (s)Frequency
\(0<t\le 3\)\(14\)
\(3<t\le 12\)\(21\)
\(12<t\le 22\)\(35\)
\(22<t\le 34\)\(35\)
\(34<t\le 38\)\(35\)

Find the cumulative frequency at \(34\) seconds.
examples.solution:
Add the frequencies up to and including the class that ends at \(34\).

\(\text{Cumulative frequency}=14+21+35+35=105\)

Answer \(105\).

examples.title: Plot the upper boundary with its cumulative frequency
examples.question:
Time (s)Frequency
\(0<t\le 5\)\(36\)
\(5<t\le 9\)\(9\)
\(9<t\le 19\)\(45\)
\(19<t\le 36\)\(45\)
\(36<t\le 38\)\(45\)

Which point is plotted for the class ending at \(9\) seconds?

  1. \((5,45)\)
  2. \((9,36)\)
  3. \((9,46)\)
  4. \((9,45)\)
examples.solution:
Use the upper boundary as the horizontal coordinate, and the running total as the vertical coordinate.

Answer \((9,45)\).

examples.title: Recover a class frequency from cumulative values
examples.question:
Class boundary (s)Cumulative frequency
\(0\)\(0\)
\(4\)\(33\)
\(11\)\(55\)
\(21\)\(110\)
\(32\)\(165\)
\(39\)\(220\)

How many times were in \(21<t\le 32\)?

lessons.title: Median, quartiles and percentiles from graphs
lessons.summary: Read quantile positions on a cumulative frequency curve and estimate the interquartile range.
lessons.objective: Read quantile positions on a cumulative frequency curve and estimate the interquartile range.
lessons.before: Read a cumulative frequency diagram and find a percentage of a quantity.
lessons.ideas:
Use \(\frac14 N,\;\frac12 N,\;\frac34 N\) for the lower quartile, median and upper quartile. For percentile \(p\), use \(\frac{p}{100}N\).

Move horizontally from the cumulative level to the curve, then vertically down to the measured axis.

Subtract the lower quartile value from the upper quartile value. At the 70th percentile about 70% of observations are at or below the estimated value.
lessons.method:
How do I find the cumulative level for a quantile?

On a cumulative frequency diagram, the final vertical value is the sample size.

Which direction do I move on the graph?

For a percentile you know the vertical level. The graph gives the observation value at that level.

How can I estimate the spread or interpret a percentile?

The IQR estimates how far apart the first and third quartile values are. A percentile reading divides the observations into approximate shares.
mistakes: A quartile level is a reading on the frequency scale. The quartile itself is a reading on the measured scale.
Reading an observation count starts from the horizontal axis. Finding a percentile reverses that direction.
Subtracting a frequency level from another yields a count, not a spread in the measured units.

examples.title: Estimate the median from a graph
examples.question: Estimate the median time in seconds to the nearest second.
examples.solution:
\(\text{Cumulative level}=\frac{50}{100}\times 140=70\)

Read across from this level and drop down to the time scale.

Answer \(22\) to the nearest whole number.

examples.title: Estimate the lower quartile from a graph
examples.question: Estimate the lower quartile time in seconds to the nearest second.
examples.solution:
\(\text{Cumulative level}=\frac{25}{100}\times 180=45\)

Read across from this level and drop down to the time scale.

Answer \(9\) to the nearest whole number.

examples.title: Read Q1 and Q3 then estimate the IQR
examples.question: Use the graph to estimate the interquartile range in seconds. Give your estimate to the nearest second.
examples.solution:
\(Q_1=11\)

\(Q_3=32\)

\(\mathrm{IQR}=32-11=21\)

Answer \(21\) to the nearest whole number.

lessons.title: Histograms and frequency density
lessons.summary: Draw unequal-width histogram bars and recover counts from their areas or from a known scale.
lessons.objective: Draw unequal-width histogram bars and recover counts from their areas or from a known scale.
lessons.before: Read class inequalities and find the area of a rectangle.
lessons.ideas:
Calculate \(\text{Frequency density}=\frac{\text{frequency}}{\text{class width}}\) for each class. Draw adjacent bars over the real class boundaries.

Multiply each bar's density by the width for its frequency. Add the relevant areas to get a total.

Find a centimetres-per-density scale from the known bar, then apply it to the other density. To estimate a count for part of a class, use the partial width under a uniform-spread assumption.
lessons.method:
Why does a histogram use frequency density?

Histogram bars cover continuous class intervals. When the widths differ, heights alone cannot represent the counts fairly.

How do I find a frequency from an existing histogram?

The bar height is its frequency density. The horizontal span shows the class width.

What if the question gives a drawn height or asks for part of a bar?

The drawing might state heights in centimetres. The ratio of two heights still equals the ratio of their densities.
mistakes: A taller but narrower bar can represent fewer observations.
Adding heights ignores the widths of the classes.
The drawn width in centimetres is not the numerical class width.

examples.title: Calculate a bar's frequency density
examples.question:

1. The values are \(7,\;8,\;13,\;36,\;6,\;7,\;12,\;32\).

    Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

    Find the median.

    [2]

  2. The values are \(7,\;8,\;12,\;32,\;6,\;7,\;10,\;13,\;36\).

    Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

    Find the range.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Order the data as \(6,\;7,\;7,\;8,\;12,\;13,\;32,\;36\).

Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

Count to the central position or average the two middle values, according to the sample size.

Answer \(10\).

(b)

Order the data as \(6,\;7,\;7,\;8,\;10,\;12,\;13,\;32,\;36\).

Use the median of each half. When the full sample has an odd length, leave its median out of the halves.

\(\text{Range}=36-6=30\)

Answer \(30\).
questions.hint_html:
(a)

Find the middle observation after ordering.

(b)

Subtract the minimum from the maximum.
questions.verification: Maths4U original. Dataset, solution and marking checked.

questions.prompt_html:
The ordered sample is \(4,\;5,\;7,\;8,\;10,\;12,\;13,\;18\). Use the medians of the lower and upper halves.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\(Q_1=6\)

\(Q_3=\frac{25}{2}\)

Answer \(\frac{13}{2}\).

(b)

\(\text{New range}=31-4=27\)

Answer \(27\).

(a)

Use the middle of each half of the ordered sample.

(b)

Update the extreme before finding the whole range.

options.A: The individual values within each interval are unknown.
options.B: The number of observations cannot be counted.
options.C: The interval boundaries do not have numbers.
options.D: Each frequency must equal its midpoint.

questions.answer_html: The individual values within each interval are unknown.

Different values within the same groups produce the same frequency table. Using midpoints assumes representative values.
